title: Mushy Peas
subtitle: The classic fish-and-chips companion
excerpt: Tinned marrowfat peas or dried marrowfat peas soaked and simmered to a thick, bright-green purée with a little butter and mint. The essential British side for fish and chips, pies, and sausages.

recipe.sourceNotes: Mushy peas are made from marrowfat peas, a variety of dried pea with a large, starchy seed that produces a thick, smooth purée when cooked. The dish has been a staple of northern English fish-and-chip shop menus since the early twentieth century, and is standard accompaniment to fish and chips, Scotch pies, and sausages in the East Midlands and the north. The traditional method uses dried marrowfat peas soaked in bicarbonate of soda overnight, which softens the skins and produces a vivid green purée; modern cooks more often use tinned marrowfat peas for convenience. The mint is a northern English addition that cuts through the starchy richness of the peas and adds a fresh note.

content.text: For tinned mushy peas (the fastest route), simply drain and heat in a saucepan, mashing lightly with a little butter and seasoning. For a homemade version using tinned marrowfat peas, drain and simmer in a little water until very soft, then mash roughly; the result has a cleaner flavour and better texture than tinned mushy peas. Either works.

items.preparation: 2 tins, drained; or use 2 tins of marrowfat peas and cook down

content.text: Drain the tinned mushy peas and put them in a small saucepan with the butter and 2 tablespoons of water. Heat over medium heat, stirring, until hot and starting to bubble. Mash lightly with a potato masher or wooden spoon: mushy peas should be rough and thick, not a smooth purée.
Season with salt and pepper. Stir in the chopped mint if using. Add more butter if a richer result is wanted. Serve immediately alongside fish and chips, pies, or sausages.
